paperReadings.note: The course publishes no slides publicly, so its course material is the per-lecture paper reading list on the site. Lecture 2's four readings (all CC BY 4.0) are transcribed in raw/papers/ from their arXiv LaTeX sources: Large Language Monkeys in full including its appendix; How Do Large Language Monkeys Get Their Power (Laws)?, Snell et al. and Archon main body only (appendices left at arXiv to save budget). Lecture 3's readings: only Weaver (Shrinking the Generation-Verification Gap with Weak Verifiers) is CC BY 4.0 and is transcribed, main body only; Cobbe et al. 2021, Lightman et al. 2023 and Math-Shepherd carry arXiv's non-exclusive licence and are linked and discussed in the wiki, not transcribed. Lecture 4's three readings (ReAct, RLEF, Constitutional AI) are all CC BY 4.0 and transcribed main body only. Lecture 5's five readings: LATS and SWiRL (CC BY 4.0) are transcribed main body only; SPRINT (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), ADaPT and Wider or Deeper? (arXiv non-exclusive) are linked and discussed, not transcribed. Lecture 6's three readings (STaR, DeepSeekMath, DAPO) all carry arXiv's non-exclusive licence and are linked and discussed in the wiki, not transcribed. Lecture 1 lists no readings. PDFs are not committed; every paper is cited at its original URL (sources.md).

figureAudit.note: false because this KB writes no descriptions of figures at all, not because descriptions went unchecked. Model-written chart descriptions were tried for lecture 2 and removed after an audit found errors in 4 of the 20 it checked. Figures are the papers' own, shown with their printed captions; state only what the caption and paper text say. All 64 crops (lecture 2: 31, lecture 3: 6, lecture 4: 17, lecture 5: 10) were verified against the PDF text layer (no text cut by the crop edge, caption complete, no body text below the caption).

caveats: PARTIAL: covers catalog lectures 1 (Course Overview), 2 (Test-Time Compute Scaling), 3 (Robust Verification), 4 (Learning from Feedback with Tools/Code), 5 (Planning and Multi-Step Reasoning) and 6 (Train Time Scaling/Scaling RL) of 9. Do not cite this KB as covering CS329A as a whole.
Lecture 1 is transcript-only: the course publishes no slides and the site lists no paper readings for it.

Lecture 2's readings: three of the four (power laws, Snell et al., Archon) are transcribed main body only; their appendices are not in this KB. Lecture 2 shows two charts that are not in the transcribed text — a SWE-bench chart with a DeepSeek model the lecturer believes was DeepSeek-V3 (not in any reading) and Archon's fusion/ranking win-rate chart (in its appendix) — so those passages are cited to the transcript only.
No KB-written figure descriptions exist: the chat must not read values off a figure image; quote the caption and the paper's text.

The auto-captions garble some model and benchmark names in lecture 1's Large Language Monkeys results (about 22:34-25:42) and a term in its reasoning-model steps (about 32:00); in lecture 2 the Archon optimizer's name ('itest', about 47:23) and a percentage from a manual answer check (about 26:08). These are marked [Ed: unclear] in the edited transcripts and not restored from outside knowledge.
Lecture 2 states Archon's average improvement as 14.1%; the paper's abstract reports 15.1% (over o1, GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet). The wiki gives both.

Lecture 3's readings: three of the four (Cobbe et al. 2021, Lightman et al. 2023, Math-Shepherd) are arXiv non-exclusive licence and are NOT transcribed; the wiki cites them by section, figure and table at their arXiv URLs, and has no images of them. Weaver is transcribed main body only.

Lecture 3 differs from its readings in places, and the wiki states both: the lecture gives Weaver-at-70B as 86.2% (paper Table 3: 87.6%) and the distilled verifier as keeping 97% of accuracy with 99%+ less compute (paper: 98.2%, or 98.7% in its abstract, and 99.97%); it describes Lightman et al.'s 'convincing wrong-answer' samples as having correct final answers, where the paper defines them as reaching incorrect ones; and its claim that majority voting generalises better than the ORM holds in Lightman et al.'s Table 1 on the three AP exams but not on AMC10/12 or in aggregate.
Lecture 3's captions leave two words unclear, marked [Ed: unclear] in the edited transcript and not guessed: a term in a student question at about 16:25 and one at about 35:08 (likely 'hacking').

Lecture 4's three readings (ReAct, RLEF, Constitutional AI) are transcribed main body only; their appendices, which hold the prompts, the constitution's principles and further ablations, are not in this KB.

Lecture 4 differs from its readings in places, and the wiki states both: the lecturer says ReAct's thoughts are separate from the action space, where the paper's formalism puts them in an augmented action space; it glosses WebShop's score as covering intermediate steps, where the paper defines it by the attributes of the product chosen; and it glosses RLEF's n@k solve rate differently from the paper's definition. RLEF's own text gives the 70B model's test-set result as 38.0 where its Table 1 lists 40.1. A chart shown at about 46:50 (fine-tuning with and without RLHF across model sizes) has method names the captions garble, so the wiki does not tie it to a figure.

Lecture 5's readings: LATS and SWiRL are transcribed main body only. SPRINT (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) and ADaPT and Wider or Deeper? (arXiv non-exclusive) are NOT transcribed and have no images; the wiki cites SPRINT by section, figure and table, and summarises ADaPT and Wider or Deeper? from their abstracts only, because the recording does not discuss them.

Lecture 5 differs from its readings in places, and the wiki states both: it describes LATS's LM and self-consistency scores as added together, where the paper weights them with a hyperparameter; reflection as generated after success or failure, where the paper reflects on unsuccessful trajectories; and the paper as not analysing cost, where the version consulted (ICML 2024) has a sample-complexity and token-consumption analysis. It calls LATS's WebShop results close to human experts, which holds for the score (75.9 vs 82.1) but not the success rate (38.0 vs 59.6). LATS's HotPotQA experiments use an oracle that reports whether an answer is correct. The DeepSeek-R1 training curves shown at about 24:19 are not from any reading.

Lecture 5's captions leave some words unclear, marked [Ed: unclear] in the edited transcript and not guessed: the benchmark named on the DeepSeek-R1 training curves (about 24:19), a word in the contrast with Math-Shepherd (about 5:37), a word at about 15:40, and 'fork' twice (about 20:21 and 34:29).

Lecture 6's readings (STaR, DeepSeekMath, DAPO) all carry arXiv's non-exclusive licence: they are NOT transcribed and have no images; the wiki cites them by section, figure, table and equation at their arXiv URLs.

Lecture 6 differs from its readings in places, and the wiki states both: it places DeepSeekMath's 51.7% (and about 60% with further tricks) on AIME, where the paper reports 51.7% and 60.9% on MATH and gives no AIME score; it quotes STaR at 51.7%, which is not a STaR result; it attaches generalized advantage estimation to GRPO, where the paper uses GAE in PPO and replaces it with a group baseline; and it describes DAPO's 47-point comparison as DeepSeek-R1 distilled into Qwen 32B, where the paper's is DeepSeek-R1-Zero-Qwen-32B, RL on the base model.
Lecture 6's closing figures on the share of RL versus pre-training in frontier models (including a Grok 4 claim) are the lecturer's recollection, not from any reading.
